Do K-pop Groups Really Die at Seven? A Survival Analysis of 590 Idol Groups¶

Author: [Your Name] · Soongsil University · 21501755 AI and Data Analysis Practice · Fall 2026

Fans call it the seven-year curse: Korean idol groups supposedly fall apart right after their seventh anniversary. This tutorial collects the debut and disbandment history of every South Korean idol group with an English Wikipedia article, and uses survival analysis — the statistics of how long until something happens — to find out whether the curse is real, who it hits hardest, and whether a group's fate can be predicted on the day it debuts.

Contents

  1. Introduction: the seven-year curse
  2. Survival analysis in five minutes
  3. Data collection: 590 groups from the Wikipedia API
  4. Data cleaning: from wikitext to a survival table
  5. Exploratory data analysis
  6. Kaplan–Meier survival curves
  7. Where is the hazard highest?
  8. Hypothesis tests: gender, label, generation
  9. Cox proportional-hazards model
  10. Predicting five-year survival at debut
  11. Discussion and limitations
  12. Further reading

1. Introduction: the seven-year curse¶

In South Korea, an idol group's first exclusive contract is capped by law at seven years. The cap comes from the Korea Fair Trade Commission's 2009 standard contract for popular culture artists, written after a series of lawsuits over so-called "slave contracts" that locked trainees in for 10–13 years (KFTC, 2009; Korea JoongAng Daily). Seven years after debut, every member has to decide whether to re-sign — and the fan community has long believed that this is the moment groups break up. 2NE1, Sistar, Wonder Girls, 4Minute and Miss A all ended in or around year seven, and each time the phrase 7년 징크스 ("seven-year jinx") trended again.

Is it real? Anecdotes cut both ways: Girls' Generation, Shinhwa and BTS passed the seven-year mark and kept going, and plenty of groups disband after two or three years without ever reaching a contract renewal. Nobody seems to have counted.

Why this is a data-science problem, not just a trivia question¶

Counting turns out to be harder than it looks, for one reason: most groups haven't finished their story. If we take every group ever formed and compute the average lifespan, we silently throw away the groups that are still active — or, worse, pretend that "still active in 2026" means "ended in 2026". Both choices bias the answer. A group that debuted in 2023 cannot possibly have hit a seven-year curse yet, but it is still evidence about what happens in years one to three.

This is exactly the situation that survival analysis was invented for. Doctors face it with patients who are still alive when a study ends; engineers face it with machines that haven't failed yet; subscription businesses face it with customers who haven't churned. Idol groups are a surprisingly clean textbook case, and because the "treatment" (the seven-year contract) applies to everyone at the same moment, the data has a built-in natural experiment.

By the end of this tutorial you will know how to:

  • pull a structured dataset of ~600 entities out of Wikipedia through its official API, with caching and polite rate limiting;
  • turn messy free-text fields like 2014–2021, 2024–present into a proper survival table with censoring;
  • estimate and read Kaplan–Meier curves and hazard functions, and test group differences with the log-rank test;
  • fit a Cox proportional-hazards model to ask which factors raise the risk of disbanding;
  • build and honestly evaluate a classifier that predicts five-year survival from debut-day information.

Everything is reproducible: the collection script and the raw cache are in the repository, and every cleaning decision is made in a visible code cell with a sentence explaining why.

2. Survival analysis in five minutes¶

If you have never met survival analysis, here is everything you need for this tutorial. If you have, skip to section 3.

Three words: duration, event, censoring¶

Each subject (a group) contributes two numbers:

Meaning For an idol group
duration $T$ how long we observed the subject years from debut to disbandment, or to today
event $E$ did the thing we care about happen? 1 = disbanded, 0 = still active

A subject with $E = 0$ is right-censored: we know it survived at least $T$ years, but not how much longer it will go. Censoring is not missing data — it is partial information, and the whole machinery below exists to use it correctly.

The survival function and the Kaplan–Meier estimator¶

The survival function $S(t) = P(T > t)$ is the probability of still being active at time $t$. The Kaplan–Meier (KM) estimator builds it step by step: at every time an event happens, multiply the current survival by the fraction of groups at risk that did not disband at that moment,

$$\hat S(t) = \prod_{t_i \le t} \left(1 - \frac{d_i}{n_i}\right),$$

where $d_i$ is the number of disbandments at time $t_i$ and $n_i$ the number of groups still active (and still observed) just before $t_i$. Censored groups count in $n_i$ until they leave, then simply drop out of the denominator — that is the trick.

The hazard function¶

The hazard $h(t)$ is the instantaneous risk of disbanding at $t$, given survival up to $t$. If the seven-year curse is real, we should see a spike in the hazard around $t = 7$ — not merely a drop in $S(t)$, which happens at every age.

Comparing groups: the log-rank test¶

To ask "do big-label groups survive longer?", we compare two KM curves with the log-rank test. Its null hypothesis is that both groups share the same survival function; a small $p$-value says the curves differ by more than chance.

Many factors at once: the Cox proportional-hazards model¶

The Cox model writes the hazard as a baseline times an exponential of covariates,

$$h(t \mid x) = h_0(t)\, \exp(\beta_1 x_1 + \dots + \beta_p x_p).$$

A coefficient $\beta_j$ is read through its hazard ratio $e^{\beta_j}$: a value of 1.5 means a one-unit increase in $x_j$ raises the disbandment risk by 50 % at every point in time.

We use the Python library lifelines for all of this. For a gentle longer introduction see the lifelines Survival Analysis intro; for the real thing, Klein & Moeschberger, Survival Analysis: Techniques for Censored and Truncated Data.

3. Data collection: 590 groups from the Wikipedia API¶

Where the data comes from¶

English Wikipedia maintains four curated lists — List of South Korean idol groups (1990s / 2000s / 2010s / 2020s) — each a flat list of article links grouped under a year heading. Every linked article carries an {{Infobox musical artist}} with fields we need:

Wikipedia field What we take from it
list-page year heading debut year
years_active activity periods, e.g. 2015–present, 2014–2021, 2024–2025
label record label(s) / agency
current_members, past_members member counts
page categories South Korean boy bands / South Korean girl groups, … disestablished in 2019

Why the API and not scraping¶

Wikipedia offers a public MediaWiki API. Using it instead of parsing HTML has three advantages for a tutorial: it is explicitly allowed, it returns the raw wikitext (so the infobox is a | key = value list rather than a styled table), and the action=query endpoint accepts several titles per request, which matters more than it sounds.

The collection code lives in scripts/collect_data.py so that the notebook stays readable. Two practical lessons from writing it:

  1. Rate limits are real. The first version fetched one article per request with a 0.1 s pause and was throttled (HTTP 429 Too Many Requests) after about forty pages. Batching ten titles per request cut the total to ~60 requests and the problem disappeared.
  2. Cache the raw responses. Every API response is saved to data/raw/pages/. Re-running the script costs zero requests, and anyone can audit exactly what Wikipedia said on the collection date (30 October 2026).

The cell below shows the two parsing functions that do the real work; the script runs them over every page.

In [1]:

import warnings

plt.rcParams["figure.dpi"] = 110

DATA = Path("../data")
TODAY_YEAR = 2026          # observation cut-off: data collected 2026-10-30

The script's core is two small regular-expression parsers. The first finds | years_active = … in the infobox (fields can span multiple lines, until the next | key = or the closing }}); the second reduces the many ways editors write activity periods to a list of (start, end) spans.

In [2]:
def extract_infobox_field(wikitext: str, field: str):
    '''Return the raw value of `| field = ...` from a Wikipedia infobox.'''
    pattern = (r"^\|\s*" + re.escape(field) +
               r"\s*=\s*(.*?)(?=^\|\s*[a-z_]+\s*=|^\}\})")
    m = re.search(pattern, wikitext, re.M | re.S)
    if not m:
        return None
    val = re.sub(r"<!--.*?-->", "", m.group(1), flags=re.S)       # HTML comments
    val = re.sub(r"<ref[^>]*/>|<ref[^>]*>.*?</ref>", "", val, flags=re.S)  # citations
    return val.strip() or None


def parse_spans(text):
    '''"2014–2021, 2024–present" -> [(2014, 2021), (2024, None)]  (None = still active).'''
    if not isinstance(text, str):
        return []
    t = re.sub(r"\{\{(?:start|end)[ _]date\|(?:[a-z]+=[^|}]*\|)*(\d{4})[^}]*\}\}", r"\1", text, flags=re.I)
    t = re.sub(r"\{\{efn\|[^{}]*\}\}", "", t, flags=re.I)              # footnotes
    t = re.sub(r"\{\{(?:en|n)dash\}\}|&ndash;|--|-|—", "–", t, flags=re.I)
    m = re.fullmatch(r"\s*\{\{hlist\|(\d{4})\|(\d{4})\}\}\s*", t)      # {{hlist|2010|2015}}
    if m:
        t = f"{m.group(1)}–{m.group(2)}"
    spans = re.findall(r"(\d{4})\s*–\s*(\d{4}|present|current)?", t, flags=re.I)
    if not spans:
        m = re.fullmatch(r"\s*(\d{4})\s*", t)                            # a lone year
        spans = [(m.group(1), m.group(1))] if m else []
    return [(int(s), None if e.lower() in ("", "present", "current") else int(e)) for s, e in spans]


# Quick sanity check on the formats we actually met in the data
for example in ["2007–2017", "{{start date|2015}}–present",
                "{{hlist|2014–2021|2024–2025}}", "{{Start date|df=yes|2012}}–{{End date|df=yes|2019}}",
                "1994–2018; 2024", "2008"]:
    print(f"{example:55} -> {parse_spans(example)}")

2007–2017                                               -> [(2007, 2017)]
{{start date|2015}}–present                             -> [(2015, None)]
{{hlist|2014–2021|2024–2025}}                           -> [(2014, 2021), (2024, 2025)]
{{Start date|df=yes|2012}}–{{End date|df=yes|2019}}     -> [(2012, 2019)]
1994–2018; 2024                                         -> [(1994, 2018)]
2008                                                    -> [(2008, 2008)]

4. Data cleaning: from wikitext to a survival table¶

Raw Wikipedia fields are written by thousands of editors with no schema. Turning them into a survival table means making a handful of decisions, each of which could change the answer, so we state every one.

4.1 Defining "debut" and "end"¶

  • Time origin = the year heading on the Wikipedia list page. The infobox years_active sometimes starts earlier (e.g. a band that existed before re-debuting as an idol group). The list page is curated specifically as idol debut year, so it is the more consistent clock.
  • Event = the end of the first continuous activity period. Lovelyz: 2014–2021, 2024–2025 is a group that disbanded in 2021 (event, $T = 7$) and later reunited. For the question "does the seven-year contract end groups?", the first ending is what matters; reunions get their own flag.
  • Censoring = the first period runs to "present". Those groups contribute $T = 2026 - \text{debut}$ with $E = 0$.
  • Resolution is one year. Wikipedia rarely gives exact dates in years_active, so a group that debuted and disbanded in the same calendar year has $T = 0$. We follow the usual mid-year convention and record such cases as $T = 0.5$ so they are not lost from the risk set.
In [5]:
df = raw.copy()
df["spans"] = df["raw_years_active"].apply(parse_spans)

# The first activity period decides the event; later periods are reunions.
first_span = df["spans"].apply(lambda s: s[0] if s else (None, None))
df["first_end_year"] = first_span.apply(lambda s: s[1])
df["first_is_open"]  = first_span.apply(lambda s: s[0] is not None and s[1] is None)
df["reunited"]       = df["spans"].apply(len).gt(1)

# Groups whose article has no usable years_active cannot enter a survival table.
no_info = df["spans"].apply(len).eq(0)
print(f"Dropping {no_info.sum()} groups with no parsable activity period: "
      f"{df.loc[no_info, 'title'].tolist()}")
df = df[~no_info].copy()

df["event"]    = (~df["first_is_open"]).astype(int)
end_year       = df["first_end_year"].fillna(TODAY_YEAR)
df["duration"] = (end_year - df["debut_year"]).clip(lower=0)
df.loc[df["duration"] == 0, "duration"] = 0.5          # mid-year convention

# A first period that ends before the listed debut year is an inconsistency between
# the list page and the infobox (usually a pre-debut band). Inspect, then drop.
bad = df["first_end_year"].notna() & (df["first_end_year"] < df["debut_year"])
print(f"\n{bad.sum()} groups whose first period ends before the listed debut year:")
display(df.loc[bad, ["title", "debut_year", "raw_years_active"]])
df = df[~bad].copy()

print(f"\nSurvival table: {len(df)} groups, {df['event'].sum()} events (disbanded), "
      f"{(df['event'] == 0).sum()} censored (still active)")

4.2 Gender¶

Wikipedia's categories (South Korean boy bands, South Korean girl groups) label 91 % of groups. For the rest we try the genre field (which sometimes literally says boy band), and otherwise record unknown rather than guess. Unknowns stay in the overall analysis and are simply left out of gender comparisons.

In [6]:
def fill_gender(row):
    if isinstance(row["cat_gender"], str):
        return row["cat_gender"]
    g = str(row["genre"]).lower()
    if "girl group" in g:
        return "girl"
    if "boy band" in g or "boy group" in g:
        return "boy"
    return "unknown"

df["gender"] = df.apply(fill_gender, axis=1)
df["gender"].value_counts()

4.3 Labels and the "Big 4"¶

The label field lists every label a group ever had, Korean and overseas, in roughly chronological order (SM | Avex Trax, JYP | Warner Japan | Republic). We keep the first entry as the debut agency, strip corporate suffixes so that SM Entertainment and SM collapse together, and flag the industry's Big 4: SM, YG, JYP and HYBE (formerly Big Hit). Labels that became HYBE subsidiaries later (Pledis, Source Music) are not counted as Big 4, because at debut they were independent — a survival model must only use information available at time zero.

In [7]:
SUFFIXES = r"\s+(Entertainment|Ent\.?|Media|Music|Records|Company|Co\.?|Group|Agency|Studio|Studios|Label|Labels)$"

def debut_label(text):
    if not isinstance(text, str):
        return None
    first = text.split("|")[0]                                   # debut-era label comes first
    first = re.sub(r"\(.*?\)", "", first)                        # drop "(2010–2015)" style notes
    first = re.sub(r"^\W+|\W+$", "", first.strip())             # stray "*" or quotes
    first = re.sub(SUFFIXES, "", first, flags=re.I)
    first = re.sub(SUFFIXES, "", first, flags=re.I)             # "SM Entertainment Group" -> "SM"
    return first.strip() or None

ALIASES = {"S.M.": "SM", "Big Hit": "HYBE", "BigHit": "HYBE", "Bighit": "HYBE",
           "Big Hit Music": "HYBE", "Hybe": "HYBE", "DSP": "DSP", "Wake One": "WakeOne"}
BIG4 = {"SM", "YG", "JYP", "HYBE"}

df["debut_label"] = df["label"].apply(debut_label).replace(ALIASES)
df["big4"] = df["debut_label"].isin(BIG4)

print(f"{df['debut_label'].nunique()} distinct debut labels; "
      f"{df['big4'].sum()} Big-4 groups ({df['big4'].mean():.1%})")
df["debut_label"].value_counts().head(15)

4.4 Members and generations¶

  • Members at debut are approximated by current + past members. For an active group with no line-up changes this is exact; for others it slightly overstates the debut line-up (members who joined later are included). We accept the approximation and note it in the limitations.
  • Generation is the fan community's own periodisation of K-pop, and it maps neatly onto debut year. Boundaries follow the most common convention (see e.g. the Wikipedia article on K-pop):
Generation Debut years Era
1st ≤ 2002 H.O.T., S.E.S., Shinhwa, g.o.d
2nd 2003–2011 TVXQ, Big Bang, Girls' Generation, 2NE1
3rd 2012–2017 EXO, BTS, Twice, Blackpink
4th 2018–2022 Stray Kids, Itzy, aespa, IVE
5th 2023– Zerobaseone, RIIZE, BabyMonster
In [8]:
df["n_members"] = (df["n_current_members"].fillna(0) + df["n_past_members"].fillna(0))
df.loc[df["n_current_members"].isna() & df["n_past_members"].isna(), "n_members"] = np.nan
df.loc[df["n_members"] == 0, "n_members"] = np.nan        # an infobox with an empty member list
# Rotating-line-up projects (Gavy NJ: 86 "members") are not idol groups in the usual sense,
# and a few counts come from mis-parsed member tables. Treat > 20 as unknown.
df.loc[df["n_members"] > 20, "n_members"] = np.nan

def generation(year):
    if year <= 2002: return "1st"
    if year <= 2011: return "2nd"
    if year <= 2017: return "3rd"
    if year <= 2022: return "4th"
    return "5th"

df["generation"] = df["debut_year"].apply(generation)

surv = df[["title", "debut_year", "generation", "gender", "debut_label", "big4",
           "n_members", "duration", "event", "reunited", "first_end_year"]].reset_index(drop=True)
surv.to_csv(DATA / "processed" / "survival_table.csv", index=False)
print(f"Saved {len(surv)} rows -> data/processed/survival_table.csv")
surv.sample(10, random_state=1)

5. Exploratory data analysis¶

Before any survival model, we should know what population we are talking about. Four questions: when did these groups debut, who made them, how big are they, and — the naïve version of our main question — how long did the ones that already ended actually last?

In [10]:
# 5.1 Debuts per year, split by gender -------------------------------------------
debuts = (surv.groupby(["debut_year", "gender"]).size().unstack(fill_value=0)
          .reindex(columns=["boy", "girl", "mixed", "unknown"], fill_value=0))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(11, 4.2))
debuts.plot(kind="bar", stacked=True, ax=ax, width=0.85,
            color=[PALETTE[c] for c in debuts.columns], edgecolor="none")
for x, (gen, year) in enumerate([("2nd", 2003), ("3rd", 2012), ("4th", 2018), ("5th", 2023)]):
    pos = list(debuts.index).index(year) - 0.5
    ax.axvline(pos, color="black", lw=0.8, ls="--", alpha=0.5)
    ax.text(pos + 0.2, ax.get_ylim()[1] * 0.95, f"{gen} gen", fontsize=9, alpha=0.7)
ax.set(title="Idol-group debuts per year (groups with an English Wikipedia article)",
       xlabel="Debut year", ylabel="Groups")
ax.legend(title="", frameon=False, ncol=4, loc="upper center", bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, -0.28))
ax.tick_params(axis="x", rotation=90)
sns.despine()
plt.tight_layout()

Two things stand out. First, the sample is dominated by the 2010s — the industry's expansion phase, when survival-show groups and mid-tier agencies multiplied. Second, the boy/girl split is close to even in most years, which is good news: gender comparisons later will not be driven by one side having ten times the data.

The dip after 2020 is partly real (COVID-19 paused debuts) and partly an artefact of our source: a group that debuted last year may not have earned a Wikipedia article yet. We return to this in the limitations.

In [11]:
# 5.2 Current status by generation -----------------------------------------------
status = (surv.assign(status=np.where(surv["event"] == 1, "disbanded", "active"))
          .groupby(["generation", "status"]).size().unstack(fill_value=0))
status["total"] = status.sum(axis=1)
status["% disbanded"] = (status["disbanded"] / status["total"] * 100).round(1)

Read this table carefully, because it shows the trap we warned about. Nearly 90 % of first-generation groups have "disbanded" and only ~12 % of fifth-generation groups have — not because the industry became seven times kinder, but because fifth-generation groups have had at most three years in which to break up. A raw disbandment rate is a function of observation time, not just risk. Survival analysis is how we separate the two.

In [12]:
# 5.3 Who makes idol groups? ------------------------------------------------------
top = surv["debut_label"].value_counts().head(15)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 5))
colors = ["#C44E52" if lab in BIG4 else "#8DA0CB" for lab in top.index]
ax.barh(top.index[::-1], top.values[::-1], color=colors[::-1])
ax.set(title="Fifteen most prolific debut labels (red = Big 4)", xlabel="Groups debuted")
ax.bar_label(ax.containers[0], padding=3, fontsize=9)

print(f"Big-4 share of all groups: {surv['big4'].mean():.1%}  "
      f"({surv['big4'].sum()} of {len(surv)})")

Big-4 share of all groups: 12.8%  (75 of 587)

SM alone debuted almost three times as many groups as the runner-up, and the Big 4 together account for roughly one in eight groups in the sample. That means the "Big 4 vs. everyone else" comparison in section 8 will be unbalanced (75 vs. ~510), which is fine for a log-rank test but something to keep in mind when reading confidence bands.

In [13]:
# 5.4 Group size -----------------------------------------------------------------
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4), gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [3, 2]})

In [14]:
# 5.5 The naive answer: how long did disbanded groups last? ----------------------
ended = surv.query("event == 1")
counts = ended["duration"].round().astype(int).value_counts().sort_index()

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 4.2))
bar_colors = ["#C44E52" if y == 7 else "#8DA0CB" for y in counts.index]
ax.bar(counts.index, counts.values, color=bar_colors, width=0.8)
ax.bar_label(ax.containers[0], fontsize=8, padding=2)
ax.set(title=f"Years from debut to disbandment, {len(ended)} groups that have already ended",
       xlabel="Years active before the first disbandment / hiatus", ylabel="Groups",
       xticks=range(0, int(counts.index.max()) + 1, 1))
sns.despine()
plt.tight_layout()

share_7 = (ended["duration"].round() == 7).mean()
print(f"Median lifespan of ended groups: {ended['duration'].median():.0f} years")
print(f"Share of ended groups that lasted exactly 7 years: {share_7:.1%}")

Median lifespan of ended groups: 4 years
Share of ended groups that lasted exactly 7 years: 9.7%

Here is the first real glimpse of the curse — and it does not look quite like the legend. The most common fate of an idol group is to end early: the median group that has ended lasted four years, and years 2 and 3 alone account for almost a third of all disbandments. From there the counts fall year by year … until they stop falling. Years 5, 6 and 7 are a plateau (33, 32, 34 groups), and then the series drops off a cliff: 18 at year 8, 13 at year 9, 6 at year 10. The seven-year mark is not a spike in this chart; it is a wall — the last year in which ending is common.

But this chart is not yet an answer, for the reason section 2 explained: it only includes the groups that have already disbanded. The 237 active groups — including every group younger than seven that might still hit the wall — are missing from the denominator. And the denominator shrinks with every year: 34 disbandments among the groups that reached year seven is a very different risk from 51 disbandments among the far larger crowd that reached year two. Whether year seven is genuinely the most dangerous year is a question about the hazard, and the hazard needs both the censored groups and the shrinking risk set.

That is where part 2 begins.

6. Kaplan–Meier survival curves¶

Now the censored groups come back in. The Kaplan–Meier estimator uses every one of the 587 groups: disbanded groups contribute an event at their duration, active groups contribute "survived at least this long" and then leave the risk set.

In [15]:
from lifelines import KaplanMeierFitter

kmf = KaplanMeierFitter()
kmf.fit(surv["duration"], surv["event"], label="All idol groups")

The properly estimated median lifespan of an idol group is 6 years, two years longer than the naïve "median of groups that already ended" (4 years) from section 5 — the censored groups pull the estimate up, as they should.

Reading the curve: about 12 % of groups are gone within a year, 30 % within three, and by the seventh anniversary only 38 % are still active. The step between year 6 and year 7 is visibly the largest single drop on the curve after the first two years: $S(6) = 0.46 \to S(7) = 0.38$. After year 8 the curve flattens — a group that survives the contract wall tends to keep going.

The shaded band is the 95 % confidence interval. It is tight up to about year 8 (hundreds of groups at risk) and widens afterwards, where fewer than 150 groups remain. Anything we say about year 12+ is built on a few dozen veterans and should be read loosely.

7. Where is the hazard highest?¶

The survival curve answers "what fraction is still around at $t$?". The seven-year curse is a claim about something sharper: "given that a group has made it to year 7, how likely is it to end this year?" That is the discrete-time hazard,

$$\hat h(t) = \frac{d_t}{n_t} = \frac{\text{disbandments in year } t}{\text{groups still active at the start of year } t},$$

and lifelines exposes both numbers in kmf.event_table. Compare the numerator alone (what the bar chart in section 5 showed) with the ratio.

In [16]:
et = kmf.event_table.loc[0.5:12].copy()
haz = pd.DataFrame({"at_risk": et["at_risk"].astype(int), "events": et["observed"].astype(int)})
haz["hazard"] = haz["events"] / haz["at_risk"]
haz["se"] = np.sqrt(haz["hazard"] * (1 - haz["hazard"]) / haz["at_risk"])   # binomial standard error
haz.index = haz.index.map(lambda t: 0 if t == 0.5 else int(t))
haz.index.name = "year"

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4.3))
hi = ["#C44E52" if y == 7 else "#8DA0CB" for y in haz.index]

axes[0].bar(haz.index, haz["events"], color=hi)
axes[0].set(title="Numerator: disbandments per year", xlabel="Year since debut", ylabel="Groups",
            xticks=haz.index)

axes[1].bar(haz.index, haz["hazard"], yerr=1.96 * haz["se"], color=hi, capsize=2,
            error_kw={"lw": 0.8, "alpha": 0.6})
axes[1].set(title="Hazard: disbandments ÷ groups still active", xlabel="Year since debut",
            ylabel="P(disband this year | active)", xticks=haz.index)
axes[1].yaxis.set_major_formatter(plt.FuncFormatter(lambda v, _: f"{v:.0%}"))
sns.despine()
plt.tight_layout()

haz.assign(hazard=haz["hazard"].round(3), se=haz["se"].round(3)).T

This is the seven-year curse, and it is real. Once we divide by the shrinking number of groups still around, the plateau from section 5 turns into an unmistakable peak:

year 4 5 6 7 8 9 10
hazard 10.9 % 11.8 % 13.7 % 18.5 % 12.8 % 11.1 % 6.5 %

A group entering its seventh year has roughly a one-in-five chance of ending before the year is out — the highest risk at any age, about 50 % above the surrounding years, and well outside the error bars of years 5 and 8. The 34 disbandments at year 7 look unremarkable as a count only because just 184 groups were still alive to produce them; years 2 and 3 had 476 and 406 candidates.

Two further things the hazard shows that the raw counts hide:

  • Years 2–3 are the second danger zone (≈ 11–12 %), the failure-to-launch period when agencies cut groups that never found an audience. The first year is actually comparatively safe (7.9 %).
  • After year 8 the hazard falls fast (6.5 % at year 10, ~3 % at 11–12). A group that re-signs through the contract wall is, in effect, a different population.

8. Hypothesis tests: gender, label, generation¶

Who hits the wall hardest? We split the sample three ways and test each split with the log-rank test ($H_0$: identical survival functions). For the five-generation comparison we use its multi-group extension.

In [17]:
from lifelines.statistics import logrank_test, multivariate_logrank_test

def km_panel(ax, data, col, order, colors, title):
    '''Overlay one Kaplan-Meier curve per level of `col`.'''
    for level in order:
        d = data[data[col] == level]
        k = KaplanMeierFitter().fit(d["duration"], d["event"],
                                    label=f"{level} (n={len(d)}, median {KaplanMeierFitter().fit(d['duration'], d['event']).median_survival_time_:.0f}y)")
        k.plot_survival_function(ax=ax, ci_show=False, color=colors[level], lw=2)
    ax.axvline(7, color="grey", ls="--", lw=0.8)
    ax.set(title=title, xlabel="Years since debut", ylabel="P(still active)", xlim=(0, 15), ylim=(0, 1.02))
    ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=8.5)

gendered = surv[surv["gender"].isin(["boy", "girl"])]
surv_lab = surv.assign(label_tier=np.where(surv["big4"], "Big 4", "Other"))
GEN_COLORS = dict(zip(["1st", "2nd", "3rd", "4th", "5th"], sns.color_palette("viridis", 5)))

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(16, 4.6))
km_panel(axes[0], gendered, "gender", ["boy", "girl"], PALETTE, "By gender")
km_panel(axes[1], surv_lab, "label_tier", ["Big 4", "Other"], {"Big 4": "#C44E52", "Other": "#8DA0CB"}, "By debut label")
km_panel(axes[2], surv, "generation", ["1st", "2nd", "3rd", "4th", "5th"], GEN_COLORS, "By generation")
sns.despine()
plt.tight_layout()

# --- the tests -----------------------------------------------------------------
boy, girl = gendered[gendered["gender"] == "boy"], gendered[gendered["gender"] == "girl"]
big, other = surv[surv["big4"]], surv[~surv["big4"]]
tests = pd.DataFrame([
    {"comparison": "boy vs girl",       "test": "log-rank",
     "statistic": logrank_test(boy["duration"], girl["duration"], boy["event"], girl["event"]).test_statistic,
     "p-value":   logrank_test(boy["duration"], girl["duration"], boy["event"], girl["event"]).p_value},
    {"comparison": "Big 4 vs other",    "test": "log-rank",
     "statistic": logrank_test(big["duration"], other["duration"], big["event"], other["event"]).test_statistic,
     "p-value":   logrank_test(big["duration"], other["duration"], big["event"], other["event"]).p_value},
    {"comparison": "5 generations",     "test": "multivariate log-rank",
     "statistic": multivariate_logrank_test(surv["duration"], surv["generation"], surv["event"]).test_statistic,
     "p-value":   multivariate_logrank_test(surv["duration"], surv["generation"], surv["event"]).p_value},
]).set_index("comparison")
tests["statistic"] = tests["statistic"].round(2)
tests["p-value"] = tests["p-value"].apply(lambda p: f"{p:.2g}")
tests
Out[17]:
test statistic p-value
comparison
boy vs girl log-rank 17.58 2.8e-05
Big 4 vs other log-rank 7.61 0.0058
5 generations multivariate log-rank 14.99 0.0047

All three splits are statistically significant, and two of them are large:

  • Girl groups disband sooner ($p < 10^{-4}$). Median lifespan 5 years versus 7 for boy groups, and the gap opens early — by year 3 the curves are already far apart. The industry folklore that girl groups have "shorter shelf lives" is borne out, though the data cannot say why: contract norms, revenue models (boy groups earn more from touring and fandom goods), and member marriage/military factors all differ.
  • Big-4 groups last longer ($p \approx 0.006$). Median 8 years versus 6. The Big-4 curve stays above the rest at every age, but notice that it too drops sharply at year 7: the contract wall is a feature of the whole industry, not of small agencies.
  • Generations differ ($p \approx 0.005$), but not in a simple "things got better/worse" way. The second generation (2003–2011) was the most durable (median 8 years); the first generation ended fast (the industry had no renewal template yet); the third and fourth are in between. The fifth generation has no median yet — fewer than half its groups have ended, which is exactly the censoring story again.

Three pairwise tests also mean three chances for a false positive. A Bonferroni correction ($\alpha = 0.05/3$) changes nothing here — every $p$ is far below 0.017 — but the Cox model in the next section is the better way to ask these questions jointly.

9. Cox proportional-hazards model¶

The log-rank tests look at one factor at a time. Girl groups are also, on average, a little smaller and debuted under slightly different label mixes, so is the gender effect "really" gender? The Cox model estimates every effect while holding the others fixed:

$$h(t \mid x) = h_0(t)\,\exp\big(\beta_\text{girl}\,x_\text{girl} + \beta_\text{big4}\,x_\text{big4} + \beta_\text{members}\,x_\text{members} + \textstyle\sum_g \beta_g\,x_g\big).$$

The second generation is the reference generation; groups of unknown gender or member count are left out (520 of 587 remain).

In [18]:
from lifelines import CoxPHFitter

cox_df = (surv[surv["gender"].isin(["boy", "girl"])]
          .dropna(subset=["n_members"])
          .assign(girl=lambda d: (d["gender"] == "girl").astype(int),
                  big4=lambda d: d["big4"].astype(int)))
for g in ["1st", "3rd", "4th", "5th"]:                       # 2nd generation = reference
    cox_df[f"gen_{g}"] = (cox_df["generation"] == g).astype(int)
COVARIATES = ["girl", "big4", "n_members", "gen_1st", "gen_3rd", "gen_4th", "gen_5th"]

cph = CoxPHFitter()
cph.fit(cox_df[["duration", "event"] + COVARIATES], duration_col="duration", event_col="event")

summary = cph.summary[["exp(coef)", "exp(coef) lower 95%", "exp(coef) upper 95%", "p"]].copy()
summary.columns = ["hazard ratio", "CI low", "CI high", "p"]
print(f"n = {len(cox_df)}, events = {cox_df['event'].sum()}, concordance = {cph.concordance_index_:.3f}")
summary.round(3)

n = 520, events = 313, concordance = 0.636

          "gen_3rd": "3rd gen (vs 2nd)", "gen_4th": "4th gen (vs 2nd)", "gen_5th": "5th gen (vs 2nd)"}

            xerr=[s["hazard ratio"] - s["CI low"], s["CI high"] - s["hazard ratio"]],
            fmt="o", color="#4C72B0", ecolor="#4C72B0", capsize=3)

       xlabel="Hazard ratio (log scale)   ← safer   |   riskier →", ylim=(-0.6, len(s) - 0.4))

plt.tight_layout()

Reading the hazard ratios¶

  • Girl group: HR ≈ 1.6 — at any given age, a girl group is about 60 % more likely to disband in the next year than a boy group with the same label tier, size and generation. The gender effect survives adjustment; it is not a proxy for something else in our data.
  • Big-4 label: HR ≈ 0.5 — a Big-4 debut halves the hazard. This is the largest protective effect in the model.
  • Members: HR ≈ 0.92 per member — surprisingly, bigger groups last longer. Nine members instead of five lowers the hazard by about 30 %. Plausible mechanisms: large groups are a larger sunk investment, can keep going when one or two members leave, and the biggest groups in recent years are survival-show products with built-in fandoms. This is the one result we did not expect.
  • Generations: relative to the durable second generation, the 1st, 3rd and 4th all carry 40–80 % more hazard; the 5th-generation estimate is uncertain (wide interval) because its groups are young.

The concordance index of 0.64 says the model ranks a random pair of groups correctly 64 % of the time — meaningful structure, but a long way from prediction. Idol-group lifespans are mostly driven by things that are not in a Wikipedia infobox.

Checking the model's assumption¶

The Cox model assumes each hazard ratio is constant over time (the "proportional" in the name). lifelines can test this; a small $p$-value flags a covariate whose effect changes with age.

In [20]:
from lifelines.statistics import proportional_hazard_test

ph = proportional_hazard_test(cph, cox_df[["duration", "event"] + COVARIATES], time_transform="rank")
ph_table = ph.summary[["test_statistic", "p"]].round(3)
ph_table["proportional?"] = np.where(ph_table["p"] < 0.05, "violated", "ok")
ph_table
Out[20]:
test_statistic p proportional?
big4 1.736 0.188 ok
gen_1st 2.259 0.133 ok
gen_3rd 8.476 0.004 violated
gen_4th 3.705 0.054 ok
gen_5th 0.338 0.561 ok
girl 7.404 0.007 violated
n_members 22.449 0.000 violated

Three covariates — gender, member count and the 3rd-generation flag — fail the test. That does not make the model wrong; it means their hazard ratios are averages over time rather than constants. Looking back at the KM panel for gender in section 8 explains why: the girl/boy gap opens in years 1–5 and then the curves run roughly parallel, so the "girl" hazard ratio is larger early and smaller late.

The standard remedy is to stratify on the offending categorical variable, letting each stratum have its own baseline hazard $h_0(t)$ while still sharing the other coefficients. Doing that for gender gives a useful robustness check: if the remaining hazard ratios barely move, the conclusions are stable.

In [21]:
cph_strat = CoxPHFitter()
cph_strat.fit(cox_df[["duration", "event"] + COVARIATES], duration_col="duration",
              event_col="event", strata=["girl"])

compare = pd.DataFrame({
    "HR (pooled)":            summary["hazard ratio"].drop("girl"),
    "HR (stratified by sex)": cph_strat.summary["exp(coef)"],
}).round(3)
compare["change"] = (compare["HR (stratified by sex)"] / compare["HR (pooled)"] - 1).map("{:+.1%}".format)
compare

gen_1st 1.823 1.831 +0.4%

10. Predicting five-year survival at debut¶

Everything above is explanation. The last question is prediction: on the day a group debuts, using only what is knowable that day, can we tell whether it will still exist five years later?

Framing it as a classification problem¶

  • Population: groups that debuted in or before 2021, so that five full years are observable by our 2026 cut-off. (A 2023 debut has an unknown five-year outcome; including it would leak the censoring into the labels.)
  • Target: $y = 1$ if the first activity period lasted $\ge 5$ years (whether or not the group has since ended), else 0.
  • Features available at debut: gender, Big-4 flag, number of members, debut year, and one engineered feature — label experience, the number of groups the same agency had debuted before this one. A model is only honest if every feature would have been known at time zero; popularity measures like page views are excluded for exactly that reason.
  • Models: logistic regression (the linear baseline), a random forest, and gradient boosting, all evaluated with 5-fold stratified cross-validation on ROC-AUC. A "majority class" dummy model sets the floor.
In [22]:
from sklearn.model_selection import StratifiedKFold, cross_val_score, cross_val_predict
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier, GradientBoostingClassifier
from sklearn.dummy import DummyClassifier
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score, roc_curve, confusion_matrix, ConfusionMatrixDisplay

ml = (surv[(surv["debut_year"] <= TODAY_YEAR - 5) & surv["gender"].isin(["boy", "girl"])]
      .dropna(subset=["n_members"]).copy())
ml["y"] = (ml["duration"] >= 5).astype(int)
ml["girl"] = (ml["gender"] == "girl").astype(int)
ml["big4"] = ml["big4"].astype(int)

# Label experience: how many groups had this agency debuted before this one? (uses the full table,
# but only *earlier* debuts, so nothing from the future leaks in)
def label_experience(row):
    if pd.isna(row["debut_label"]):
        return 0
    return int(((surv["debut_label"] == row["debut_label"]) & (surv["debut_year"] < row["debut_year"])).sum())
ml["label_experience"] = ml.apply(label_experience, axis=1)

FEATURES = ["girl", "big4", "n_members", "debut_year", "label_experience"]
X, y = ml[FEATURES], ml["y"]
print(f"{len(ml)} groups debuted ≤ {TODAY_YEAR - 5}; {y.mean():.1%} survived five years")

models = {
    "Majority-class dummy": DummyClassifier(strategy="prior"),
    "Logistic regression":  make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000)),
    "Random forest":        RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=300, min_samples_leaf=5, random_state=0),
    "Gradient boosting":    GradientBoostingClassifier(n_estimators=150, max_depth=2, learning_rate=0.05, random_state=0),
}
cv = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=42)
scores = {name: cross_val_score(m, X, y, cv=cv, scoring="roc_auc") for name, m in models.items()}
pd.DataFrame({"CV ROC-AUC": {k: f"{v.mean():.3f} ± {v.std():.3f}" for k, v in scores.items()}})

400 groups debuted ≤ 2021; 60.8% survived five years
Out[22]:
CV ROC-AUC
Majority-class dummy 0.500 ± 0.000
Logistic regression 0.658 ± 0.031
Random forest 0.670 ± 0.022
Gradient boosting 0.690 ± 0.023
In [23]:
# ROC curves from out-of-fold predictions ------------------------------------------
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4.8))
oof = {}
for (name, m), color in zip(list(models.items())[1:], ["#8DA0CB", "#66C2A5", "#C44E52"]):
    oof[name] = cross_val_predict(m, X, y, cv=cv, method="predict_proba")[:, 1]
    fpr, tpr, _ = roc_curve(y, oof[name])
    axes[0].plot(fpr, tpr, color=color, lw=2, label=f"{name} (AUC {roc_auc_score(y, oof[name]):.2f})")
axes[0].plot([0, 1], [0, 1], color="grey", ls="--", lw=1, label="Chance")
axes[0].set(title="Out-of-fold ROC curves", xlabel="False positive rate", ylabel="True positive rate")
axes[0].legend(frameon=False)

best = "Gradient boosting"
cm = confusion_matrix(y, oof[best] > 0.5)
ConfusionMatrixDisplay(cm, display_labels=["ended < 5y", "survived ≥ 5y"]).plot(ax=axes[1], colorbar=False, cmap="Blues")
axes[1].set(title=f"{best}: out-of-fold predictions at 0.5 threshold")
sns.despine()
plt.tight_layout()

acc = ((oof[best] > 0.5) == y).mean()
print(f"{best}: out-of-fold accuracy {acc:.1%} vs. majority baseline {y.mean():.1%}")

Gradient boosting: out-of-fold accuracy 64.2% vs. majority baseline 60.8%

What the model knows, and what it doesn't¶

Gradient boosting reaches an out-of-fold ROC-AUC of about 0.69, logistic regression about 0.66, and the dummy model 0.50. So debut-day information carries real signal — a 0.69 AUC means the model ranks a random surviving group above a random failed one about 69 % of the time — but nowhere near enough to call individual outcomes: accuracy at the 0.5 threshold is only a few points above simply predicting "survives" for everyone, and the confusion matrix shows the model is reluctant to predict failure at all.

Which features do the work? Permutation importance shuffles one feature at a time and measures how much AUC is lost.

In [24]:
from sklearn.inspection import permutation_importance

# Importance must be measured on data the model has NOT seen, or it rewards memorisation:
# refit on each training fold, shuffle features on the matching test fold, average over folds.
fold_imps = []
for train_idx, test_idx in cv.split(X, y):
    gb = GradientBoostingClassifier(n_estimators=150, max_depth=2, learning_rate=0.05, random_state=0)
    gb.fit(X.iloc[train_idx], y.iloc[train_idx])
    perm = permutation_importance(gb, X.iloc[test_idx], y.iloc[test_idx],
                                  scoring="roc_auc", n_repeats=30, random_state=0)
    fold_imps.append(perm.importances_mean)
fold_imps = pd.DataFrame(fold_imps, columns=FEATURES)
imp = fold_imps.mean().sort_values()

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4.2), gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [2, 3]})
axes[0].barh(imp.index, imp.values, xerr=fold_imps.std()[imp.index], color="#8DA0CB", capsize=3)
axes[0].axvline(0, color="grey", lw=0.8)
axes[0].set(title="Permutation importance (AUC lost)", xlabel="Δ ROC-AUC when shuffled")

# Five-year survival rate by member count — the model's strongest signal, shown raw
rate = (ml.assign(size=pd.cut(ml["n_members"], [0, 3, 5, 7, 9, 20],
                              labels=["1–3", "4–5", "6–7", "8–9", "10+"]))
          .groupby("size", observed=True)["y"].agg(["mean", "size"]))
axes[1].bar(rate.index, rate["mean"], color="#66C2A5")
for i, (m_, n_) in enumerate(zip(rate["mean"], rate["size"])):
    axes[1].text(i, m_ + 0.015, f"n={n_}", ha="center", fontsize=9)
axes[1].axhline(y.mean(), color="grey", ls="--", lw=1)
axes[1].set(title="Five-year survival rate by group size", xlabel="Members at debut", ylabel="Survived ≥ 5 years",
            ylim=(0, 1))
axes[1].yaxis.set_major_formatter(plt.FuncFormatter(lambda v, _: f"{v:.0%}"))
sns.despine()
plt.tight_layout()

Two features carry most of the predictive power: group size and debut year. The Big-4 flag and label experience each add a little. Gender adds nothing — shuffling it changes the AUC by less than the fold-to-fold noise.

That last result deserves a pause, because gender had the second-largest effect in the Cox model ($\text{HR} \approx 1.6$, $p < 0.001$). There is no contradiction: explanation and prediction are different questions. A hazard ratio of 1.6 is a strong, reliable average difference between two large populations; but the two populations overlap so much that knowing a group's gender barely moves the odds for any individual group. Significance tells you an effect is real; it does not tell you it is useful for forecasting.

The right-hand panel shows the size effect without any model: duos and trios survive five years less than half the time, groups of eight or more about three-quarters of the time.

The honest summary is that a K-pop group's fate is only weakly predictable at debut. That is not a failure of the analysis — it is the finding. Survival is decided by what happens after debut: a hit song, a viral moment, a scandal, members' individual choices at year seven. None of that is in the infobox, and most of it is not predictable from anything.

11. Discussion and limitations¶

What we found¶

  1. The seven-year curse is real, and it is a hazard peak, not a myth. A group entering its seventh year has an 18.5 % chance of ending that year, the highest at any age and roughly 1.5× the risk in years 5–6 and 8–9. The peak coincides exactly with the legal maximum length of a first exclusive contract, which is the obvious mechanism.
  2. It is not the main way groups die. Most disbandments happen in years 1–4; the median group lasts six years and never reaches the contract wall. Years 2–3 are a second, broader danger zone.
  3. Girl groups face about 60 % higher hazard than boy groups at every age, after adjusting for label and size. Big-4 groups face about half the hazard of everyone else. Larger groups last longer — the one result we did not anticipate.
  4. Debut-day information predicts five-year survival only modestly (AUC ≈ 0.69). Most of what determines a group's lifespan happens after it debuts.

What to be careful about¶

  • Selection bias from the source. Only groups with an English Wikipedia article are in the data. That rule systematically excludes the groups most likely to fail quickly and quietly, so our hazard in years 0–2 is probably an underestimate, and recent debuts (2024–26) are under-counted until they earn an article. Every survival number here should be read as "among groups notable enough to be documented".
  • One-year resolution. Wikipedia's years_active rarely gives months. A group that debuted in January 2015 and disbanded in December 2021 and one that debuted in December 2015 and disbanded in January 2021 both get $T = 6$. This blurs, but cannot create, a peak at year 7.
  • "Disbanded" is Wikipedia's judgement. We treat the end of the first activity period as the event; indefinite hiatuses, label disputes and quiet fade-outs are all recorded differently by different editors. The 54 groups flagged reunited show that "ended" is not always final.
  • Member count is approximate (current + past members, so later additions are counted) and we dropped seven implausible values above 20.
  • The Big-4 flag is defined at debut, which is correct for a survival model but means Pledis (Seventeen, fromis_9) and Source Music (GFriend, Le Sserafim) count as "other" even though HYBE later acquired them.
  • Proportional hazards are violated for gender and size, so their hazard ratios are time-averaged; the stratified check suggests the conclusions are stable, but a time-varying-coefficient model would be the next step.

What would make it better¶

Exact debut and disbandment dates (available from Korean-language sources such as Namuwiki or the Korea Music Content Association), first-year chart performance as a post-debut covariate, and a competing-risks treatment that separates "disbanded" from "indefinite hiatus" would each sharpen the picture. The pipeline here — list page → infobox → survival table — would need no structural change to absorb any of them.

12. Further reading¶

Survival analysis

  • lifelines documentation — the library used throughout; its Survival Analysis intro and Survival Regression pages are the best short tutorials available.
  • Klein, J. P. & Moeschberger, M. L. (2003). Survival Analysis: Techniques for Censored and Truncated Data, 2nd ed. Springer. The standard graduate text.
  • Bland, J. M. & Altman, D. G. (2004). "The logrank test." BMJ 328:1073. doi:10.1136/bmj.328.7447.1073 — a one-page explanation.
  • Therneau, T. & Grambsch, P. (2000). Modeling Survival Data: Extending the Cox Model. Springer — for the proportional-hazards diagnostics used in section 9.
  • Davidson-Pilon, C. (2019). "lifelines: survival analysis in Python." Journal of Open Source Software 4(40):1317. doi:10.21105/joss.01317

Machine learning and evaluation

  • scikit-learn user guide: cross-validation, permutation importance, ROC curves.
  • Kuhn, M. & Johnson, K. (2019). Feature Engineering and Selection. CRC Press. On why "features known at prediction time" matters.

Data and APIs

  • MediaWiki API: Main page and API etiquette — the rules we followed in section 3.
  • Wikipedia: List of South Korean idol groups.
  • Wikimedia REST API pageviews — a natural source for a popularity covariate in a follow-up.

The K-pop industry

  • Korea Fair Trade Commission (2009). Standard exclusive contract for popular culture artists (대중문화예술인 표준전속계약서) — the origin of the seven-year limit. Korean overview on the KFTC site.
  • Wikipedia, K-pop § Generations for the generation boundaries used in section 4.
  • Lie, J. (2015). K-Pop: Popular Music, Cultural Amnesia, and Economic Innovation in South Korea. University of California Press — on the trainee/contract system.
  • Korea Creative Content Agency (KOCCA), annual Music Industry White Paper (음악산업백서) — industry statistics.
